courses.description: This course introduces learners to the fundamentals of Agentic AI and modern AI agent systems. Learners will understand the difference between traditional AI, generative AI, and agentic AI, and explore how agents use reasoning, planning, tools, memory, and feedback to accomplish complex tasks. The course covers agent architectures, tool calling, workflows, autonomous decision-making, and multi-agent collaboration. Learners will also gain hands-on experience building simple AI agents using frameworks such as LangChain and LangGraph. By the end of the course, learners will be able to explain core agentic AI concepts, design basic agent workflows, integrate tools with agents, and identify suitable real-world enterprise use cases for agentic systems.

courses.description:
Generative AI & Enterprise LLM Architecture is a comprehensive masterclass engineered for senior developers, architects, and technical leaders who want to build secure, scalable, and hallucination-free AI applications.

Key Learning Outcomes: -RAG Pipeline Design:Build robust Retrieval-Augmented Generation architectures using vector stores (pgvector/Qdrant) and chunking strategies -Enterprise Security & Safety:Implement guardrails against prompt injection, jailbreaks, data leakage, and ungrounded hallucinations. -Model Evaluation & Fine-Tuning: Evaluate model outputs programmatically using Ragas, BLEU, and LLM-as-a-Judge frameworks. -Production Deployment:Scale LLM endpoints using asynchronous worker queues, response streaming (SSE), and intelligent semantic caching.

Title: Introduction to Agentic AI

Article Content:

Agentic AI represents a new generation of artificial intelligence systems that can understand goals, reason about tasks, make decisions, use external tools, and take actions with limited human intervention.

Unlike traditional AI systems that typically respond to a predefined request, AI agents can follow a multi-step process to accomplish a goal. An agent may analyze the user's request, create a plan, retrieve information, call an API or tool, evaluate the result, and decide what to do next.

Key Components of Agentic AI

1. Reasoning
Agents analyze information and determine the appropriate next step based on the given goal.

2. Planning
An agent can break a complex task into smaller, manageable steps and execute them in sequence.

3. Tool Usage
Agents can interact with external tools such as databases, APIs, search engines, calculators, and business applications.

4. Memory
Memory allows an agent to maintain relevant information from previous interactions and use it when making future decisions.

5. Decision Making
Agents evaluate available information and select an appropriate action to achieve their objectives.

Example

Consider an employee asking:

"Find my remaining leave balance and suggest suitable dates for a vacation."

An Agentic AI system could identify the employee, retrieve leave information from an HR system, check the company holiday calendar, analyze available dates, and provide suitable recommendations.

Agentic AI vs Generative AI

Generative AI primarily focuses on generating content such as text, images, code, or summaries in response to prompts. Agentic AI goes a step further by using AI models as part of a larger system that can reason, plan, interact with tools, and perform actions.

Agentic AI is therefore useful for applications such as customer support, enterprise automation, financial analysis, software development, research assistants, and workflow automation.

Key Takeaway

Agentic AI enables AI systems to move from simply answering questions to achieving goals through reasoning, planning, tool usage, and actions. Understanding these concepts is the foundation for building reliable and useful AI agents.

learningContents.description:
Docker: A Simple Guide to Containers and Application Deployment

Docker is one of the most widely used tools for modern software development. It helps developers package an application together with everything it needs to run and then execute that application in an isolated environment called a container.

The main problem Docker solves is simple:

“It works on my machine, but it doesn't work on yours.”

A developer may build an application using a particular version of Python, Node.js, Java, libraries, environment variables, and system dependencies. When another developer runs the same application on a different machine, something may fail because the environment is different.

Docker solves this by allowing the application and its dependencies to be packaged into a standardized image and run as a container. Docker describes a container as a runnable instance of an image, while an image is a standardized package containing the files, binaries, libraries, and configuration needed to run an application.

1. What Is Docker?

Docker is a platform for developing, shipping, and running applications.

Instead of installing everything directly on your computer, you can package your application into a Docker image.

For example, imagine you have a Python application.

Without Docker, your machine might need:

Python 3.12
Flask
NumPy
Pandas
specific operating-system libraries
environment variables
your application code

You would have to install all of these manually.

With Docker, you can describe the environment in a Dockerfile:

Python
   +
Libraries
   +
Application Code
   +
Configuration
       ↓
   Docker Image
       ↓
   Container
       ↓
Running Application

The result is a much more consistent environment between development, testing, and production.

Docker's platform is designed around packaging applications into containers, which can then be developed, tested, shared, and deployed across different environments.

2. Why Do We Need Docker?

Before understanding Docker technically, it is useful to understand the problem it solves.

Imagine a team building an AI application.

Developer A has:

Python 3.12
PyTorch 2.x
FastAPI
NumPy
CUDA libraries

Developer B has:

Python 3.10
Different PyTorch version
Different NumPy version
Different OS libraries

The application works on A's machine but fails on B's machine.

This can happen because of:

different programming-language versions
different library versions
missing dependencies
operating-system differences
configuration differences
environment-variable differences

Docker allows the team to define the environment once and package it.

Then:

Developer Machine
       ↓
Docker Container

Testing Server
       ↓
Docker Container

Cloud Server
       ↓
Docker Container

The application runs inside a controlled environment rather than depending heavily on what is installed on the host.

3. Docker vs Virtual Machines

Docker containers are often compared with virtual machines.

A traditional virtual-machine architecture looks like:

Physical Machine
       ↓
Host Operating System
       ↓
Hypervisor
       ↓
Virtual Machine
       ↓
Guest Operating System
       ↓
Application

A Docker architecture is generally more lightweight:

Physical Machine
       ↓
Host Operating System
       ↓
Docker Engine
       ↓
Container
       ↓
Application

A virtual machine normally includes an entire guest operating system.

A container shares the host's operating-system kernel while isolating processes, filesystems, networking, and other resources.

Docker uses Linux kernel technologies such as namespaces and cgroups to provide isolation and resource control.

This is one reason containers can be lightweight compared with full virtual machines.

4. What Is a Container?

A container is a running instance of a Docker image.

Think of an image as a blueprint and a container as the running thing created from that blueprint.

For example:

Docker Image
     ↓
     ↓ docker run
     ↓
Docker Container

Suppose you have an image called:

my-python-app

You can create a container from it:

docker run my-python-app

Docker starts a container based on the image.

You can have multiple containers created from the same image:

             Docker Image
                  │
       ┌──────────┼──────────┐
       ↓          ↓          ↓
 Container 1  Container 2  Container 3

Each container can have its own configuration, network settings, storage, and lifecycle.

5. What Is a Docker Image?

A Docker image is a read-only package used to create containers.

It contains everything required for an application to run, such as:

application code
runtime
libraries
dependencies
configuration
filesystem content

Docker images are built in layers. Each Dockerfile instruction can contribute a layer, and Docker can reuse unchanged layers when rebuilding an image.

For example:

Base Python Image
        ↓
Install Dependencies
        ↓
Copy Application
        ↓
Configure Application
        ↓
Docker Image

This layered structure also helps Docker use build cache efficiently.

6. Image vs Container

This is one of the most important concepts to understand.

Image	Container
Blueprint/template	Running instance
Read-only	Has a writable runtime layer
Used to create containers	Runs the application
Can be stored in a registry	Runs on a Docker host
Doesn't represent a running process	Represents a running process

A simple analogy:

Image = Class
Container = Object

Or:

Image = Recipe
Container = Prepared dish

You create an image once and can create many containers from it.

7. Dockerfile

A Dockerfile is a text file containing instructions that Docker uses to build an image.

A simple Python Dockerfile might look like:

FROM python:3.12

WORKDIR /app

COPY requirements.txt .

RUN pip install -r requirements.txt

COPY . .

CMD ["python", "app.py"]

Let's understand it line by line.

FROM
FROM python:3.12

This specifies the base image.

Docker will start with a Python 3.12 environment.

WORKDIR
WORKDIR /app

This sets the working directory inside the image/container.

COPY
COPY requirements.txt .

This copies the dependency file into the image.

Then:

COPY . .

copies the application files.

RUN
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt

This executes a command while building the image.

CMD
CMD ["python", "app.py"]

This defines the default command executed when the container starts.

Docker documents FROM, RUN, COPY, WORKDIR, and CMD among the common Dockerfile instructions.

8. Building a Docker Image

Suppose your project looks like:

myapp/
│
├── app.py
├── requirements.txt
└── Dockerfile

You can build an image:

docker build -t myapp .

Here:

docker build

means build an image.

-t myapp

gives the image a name/tag.

.

means the current directory is the build context.

Docker uses the Dockerfile and files available in that build context to construct the image.

9. Running a Container

After building the image:

docker run myapp

Docker creates and starts a container from the image.

The flow is:

Dockerfile
    ↓
docker build
    ↓
Docker Image
    ↓
docker run
    ↓
Docker Container
    ↓
Application Running

This is the fundamental Docker workflow.

10. Useful Docker Commands

Some basic commands are:

Check Docker version
docker --version
List images
docker images
Run a container
docker run myapp
List running containers
docker ps
List all containers
docker ps -a
Stop a container
docker stop <container-id>
Start a stopped container
docker start <container-id>
Remove a container
docker rm <container-id>
Remove an image
docker rmi <image-id>

These commands allow developers to manage the basic lifecycle of Docker images and containers. Docker's documentation also uses docker ps for viewing running containers and docker stop for stopping them.

11. Docker Ports

Suppose your application runs on port 5000 inside the container.

The application is isolated inside the container, so you need to publish the port to access it from your machine.

For example:

docker run -p 5000:5000 myapp

The format is:

host-port : container-port

So:

5000:5000

means:

Your Computer
localhost:5000
       ↓
Docker Container
port 5000
       ↓
Application

Docker can publish container ports to the host so that applications can be accessed externally.

12. Docker Volumes

Containers are designed to be replaceable.

If important data exists only inside a container and that container is deleted, that data can disappear.

For persistent data, Docker provides volumes.

For example, a database container may use a volume:

Database Container
       ↓
Docker Volume
       ↓
Persistent Data

Even if you remove the container, the volume can preserve the data.

This is particularly important for:

databases
uploaded files
application data
logs
persistent storage

Docker supports storage mechanisms for persisting data outside the writable container layer.

13. Docker Networks

Containers often need to communicate with each other.

Imagine a web application consisting of:

Frontend
   ↓
Backend API
   ↓
Database

Each could run in its own container:

Frontend Container
        ↓
Backend Container
        ↓
Database Container

Docker networks allow these containers to communicate.

For example:

frontend
   │
   │ HTTP
   ↓
backend
   │
   │ database connection
   ↓
mysql

This separation is useful in microservice architectures.

14. Docker Compose

Real applications often need more than one container.

For example:

React Frontend
      +
Node.js Backend
      +
MySQL
      +
Redis

Running each container manually can become inconvenient.

Docker Compose allows you to define multi-container applications in a Compose file.

Conceptually:

docker-compose.yml
        ↓
 ┌──────┼─────────┐
 ↓      ↓         ↓
Web   Backend   Database

You can define:

services
networks
volumes
environment variables
ports

Then start the application stack using Docker Compose.

Docker's current learning path includes Compose specifically for multi-container applications.

15. Example Docker Compose Application

Imagine an application with:

Frontend
Backend
MySQL

A simplified Compose file might look like:

services:

  frontend:
    build: ./frontend
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"

  backend:
    build: ./backend
    ports:
      - "5000:5000"

  database:
    image: mysql:8

Now instead of manually starting three containers, you can manage the application as one multi-service stack.

The architecture becomes:

                  Docker Compose
                        │
          ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
          ↓             ↓             ↓
      Frontend       Backend       MySQL
      Container      Container     Container
16. Docker Registry

A Docker registry is a place where Docker images can be stored and distributed.

One popular registry is Docker Hub.

The workflow becomes:

Developer
   ↓
Dockerfile
   ↓
docker build
   ↓
Image
   ↓
docker push
   ↓
Docker Registry
   ↓
docker pull
   ↓
Production Server

This allows teams to share container images.

Docker documentation describes a registry as a place where Docker images are stored, and Docker Hub is the default public registry used by Docker in many workflows.

17. Docker Image Tags

Images can have tags.

For example:

myapp:1.0
myapp:2.0
myapp:latest

A tag helps identify a particular version.

For production systems, version-specific tags are often preferable to relying only on latest.

For example:

company/backend:1.4.2

is much clearer than:

company/backend:latest

because you know exactly which version you're deploying.

18. Docker and CI/CD

Docker is very useful in CI/CD pipelines.

Imagine a development workflow:

Developer
    ↓
Git Push
    ↓
GitHub
    ↓
CI Pipeline
    ↓
Build Docker Image
    ↓
Run Tests
    ↓
Push Image
    ↓
Deploy

Because the application is packaged consistently, the same image can move through:

Development
      ↓
Testing
      ↓
Staging
      ↓
Production

Docker specifically highlights containers as useful for continuous integration and continuous delivery workflows.

19. Docker in Machine Learning

Docker is also very useful for Machine Learning and AI projects.

Suppose an ML project requires:

Python 3.12
PyTorch
Transformers
CUDA
FastAPI
NumPy
Pandas

Installing all of these manually can cause environment problems.

Docker can package the environment:

Docker Image
│
├── Python
├── PyTorch
├── Transformers
├── NumPy
├── Pandas
├── FastAPI
└── ML Application

Then the same environment can be used during development and deployment.

For ML teams, this can be particularly useful when multiple developers need compatible environments.

20. Docker for Microservices

Docker fits naturally with microservice architectures.

Instead of building one huge application:

Large Monolithic Application

you can separate services:

                Application
                     │
        ┌────────────┼─────────────┐
        ↓            ↓             ↓
   User Service  Payment       Notification
                  Service        Service
        ↓            ↓             ↓
   Container      Container     Container

Each service can have:

its own dependencies
its own image
its own container
its own deployment lifecycle

This makes Docker useful for distributed systems.

21. Docker Security

Containers provide isolation, but Docker containers should not automatically be considered completely secure.

Developers should follow security practices such as:

use trusted base images
keep images updated
scan images for vulnerabilities
avoid unnecessary packages
don't store secrets directly in Dockerfiles
use non-root users where appropriate
limit container permissions
avoid exposing unnecessary ports
use minimal base images where practical

For example, instead of running an application as root, Docker's documentation demonstrates using a dedicated application user in Dockerfiles.

22. Dockerfile Best Practices

A good Dockerfile should be:

small
reproducible
secure
easy to understand
efficient to rebuild

For example, instead of copying everything immediately:

COPY . .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt

you can first copy dependency files:

COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt

COPY . .

Why?

Docker builds images in layers and can reuse cached layers when earlier instructions haven't changed.

If your source code changes but requirements.txt doesn't, Docker may be able to reuse the dependency-installation layer.

This can make builds faster.

23. Multi-Stage Builds

For some applications, you don't need development tools in the final production image.

For example:

Stage 1
Build Application
     ↓
Stage 2
Production Image

The first stage can contain:

compilers
development dependencies
build tools

The final stage contains only what is needed to run the application.

This can produce smaller and cleaner production images.

Docker's current documentation includes multi-stage builds as a technique for optimizing image construction.

24. Docker and Kubernetes

Docker and Kubernetes are related, but they are not the same thing.

Docker primarily provides tools for building and running containers.

Kubernetes is a platform for managing containerized workloads across clusters.

A simplified relationship is:

Docker
│
├── Build Image
├── Run Container
├── Manage Images
└── Container Development
             ↓
        Kubernetes
             ↓
   Manage many workloads
             ↓
    Multiple Machines

Kubernetes can manage things such as:

scaling
service discovery
deployments
health checks
container scheduling
rolling updates

So you can think:

Docker helps package and run applications; Kubernetes helps operate containerized applications at scale.

25. Docker's Complete Workflow

A typical Docker development lifecycle looks like this:

1. Write Application
        ↓
2. Create Dockerfile
        ↓
3. docker build
        ↓
4. Docker Image
        ↓
5. docker run
        ↓
6. Container
        ↓
7. Test Application
        ↓
8. docker tag
        ↓
9. docker push
        ↓
10. Container Registry
        ↓
11. Production

This workflow is one of the major reasons Docker became popular in modern application development.

26. A Simple Real-World Example

Imagine a company develops an employee learning platform.

The platform contains:

Next.js Frontend
Node.js Backend
MySQL Database
Redis

Without containers, developers might need to install all of these locally.

With Docker:

                 LMS Application
                       │
          ┌────────────┼────────────┐
          ↓            ↓            ↓
       Frontend      Backend       MySQL
       Container     Container     Container
                       │
                       ↓
                     Redis
                    Container

Docker Compose can define these services.

Now a developer can clone the project and start the environment using the project's container configuration instead of manually installing every dependency.

This creates a much more consistent development environment.

27. Common Docker Mistakes

Beginners often make several mistakes.

Mistake 1: Using huge images

A large image takes more storage and can take longer to transfer.

Mistake 2: Storing secrets in Dockerfiles

Never put things such as:

API_KEY=secret
PASSWORD=123456

directly into an image.

Mistake 3: Running everything as root

Use an appropriate non-root user when possible.

Mistake 4: Treating containers like virtual machines

Containers are not complete virtual machines.

Mistake 5: Storing database data only inside the container

Use persistent storage.

Mistake 6: Using latest everywhere

Versioned image tags make deployments easier to reproduce.

Mistake 7: Putting unnecessary files into the build context

A .dockerignore file can prevent unnecessary files from being sent to the builder.

28. Docker in Simple Words

If you remember only five things, remember these:

1. Dockerfile

Instructions for building an image.

2. Image

Package containing everything needed to run an application.

3. Container

Running instance of an image.

4. Registry

Place where images are stored and shared.

5. Docker Compose

Tool for managing applications made of multiple containers.

The basic relationship is:

                 Dockerfile
                     │
                     │ docker build
                     ↓
                Docker Image
                     │
                     │ docker run
                     ↓
               Docker Container
                     │
                     ↓
              Running Application
29. Final Takeaway

Docker is fundamentally about packaging applications consistently and running them in isolated environments.

Instead of saying:

"Install Python 3.12, install these 20 libraries, configure these environment variables, install this system dependency, and then run the application."

you can define the environment in a Dockerfile and build an image.

That image can then be used to create containers.

The overall idea is:

Application
    +
Dependencies
    +
Runtime
    +
Configuration
        ↓
    Docker Image
        ↓
    Container
        ↓
Running Application

This makes applications easier to develop, test, share, and deploy. Docker's official learning path covers the same progression: containers and images first, then Dockerfiles, building images, publishing them, and multi-container applications with Compose.

Docker: A Simple Guide to Containers and Application Deployment

Docker is one of the most widely used tools for modern software development. It helps developers package an application together with everything it needs to run and then execute that application in an isolated environment called a container.

The main problem Docker solves is simple:

“It works on my machine, but it doesn't work on yours.”

A developer may build an application using a particular version of Python, Node.js, Java, libraries, environment variables, and system dependencies. When another developer runs the same application on a different machine, something may fail because the environment is different.

Docker solves this by allowing the application and its dependencies to be packaged into a standardized image and run as a container. Docker describes a container as a runnable instance of an image, while an image is a standardized package containing the files, binaries, libraries, and configuration needed to run an application.

1. What Is Docker?

Docker is a platform for developing, shipping, and running applications.

Instead of installing everything directly on your computer, you can package your application into a Docker image.

For example, imagine you have a Python application.

Without Docker, your machine might need:

Python 3.12
Flask
NumPy
Pandas
specific operating-system libraries
environment variables
your application code

You would have to install all of these manually.

With Docker, you can describe the environment in a Dockerfile:

Python
   +
Libraries
   +
Application Code
   +
Configuration
       ↓
   Docker Image
       ↓
   Container
       ↓
Running Application

The result is a much more consistent environment between development, testing, and production.

Docker's platform is designed around packaging applications into containers, which can then be developed, tested, shared, and deployed across different environments.

2. Why Do We Need Docker?

Before understanding Docker technically, it is useful to understand the problem it solves.

Imagine a team building an AI application.

Developer A has:

Python 3.12
PyTorch 2.x
FastAPI
NumPy
CUDA libraries

Developer B has:

Python 3.10
Different PyTorch version
Different NumPy version
Different OS libraries

The application works on A's machine but fails on B's machine.

This can happen because of:

different programming-language versions
different library versions
missing dependencies
operating-system differences
configuration differences
environment-variable differences

Docker allows the team to define the environment once and package it.

Then:

Developer Machine
       ↓
Docker Container

Testing Server
       ↓
Docker Container

Cloud Server
       ↓
Docker Container

The application runs inside a controlled environment rather than depending heavily on what is installed on the host.

3. Docker vs Virtual Machines

Docker containers are often compared with virtual machines.

A traditional virtual-machine architecture looks like:

Physical Machine
       ↓
Host Operating System
       ↓
Hypervisor
       ↓
Virtual Machine
       ↓
Guest Operating System
       ↓
Application

A Docker architecture is generally more lightweight:

Physical Machine
       ↓
Host Operating System
       ↓
Docker Engine
       ↓
Container
       ↓
Application

A virtual machine normally includes an entire guest operating system.

A container shares the host's operating-system kernel while isolating processes, filesystems, networking, and other resources.

Docker uses Linux kernel technologies such as namespaces and cgroups to provide isolation and resource control.

This is one reason containers can be lightweight compared with full virtual machines.

4. What Is a Container?

A container is a running instance of a Docker image.

Think of an image as a blueprint and a container as the running thing created from that blueprint.

For example:

Docker Image
     ↓
     ↓ docker run
     ↓
Docker Container

Suppose you have an image called:

my-python-app

You can create a container from it:

docker run my-python-app

Docker starts a container based on the image.

You can have multiple containers created from the same image:

             Docker Image
                  │
       ┌──────────┼──────────┐
       ↓          ↓          ↓
 Container 1  Container 2  Container 3

Each container can have its own configuration, network settings, storage, and lifecycle.

5. What Is a Docker Image?

A Docker image is a read-only package used to create containers.

It contains everything required for an application to run, such as:

application code
runtime
libraries
dependencies
configuration
filesystem content

Docker images are built in layers. Each Dockerfile instruction can contribute a layer, and Docker can reuse unchanged layers when rebuilding an image.

For example:

Base Python Image
        ↓
Install Dependencies
        ↓
Copy Application
        ↓
Configure Application
        ↓
Docker Image

This layered structure also helps Docker use build cache efficiently.

6. Image vs Container

This is one of the most important concepts to understand.

Image	Container
Blueprint/template	Running instance
Read-only	Has a writable runtime layer
Used to create containers	Runs the application
Can be stored in a registry	Runs on a Docker host
Doesn't represent a running process	Represents a running process

A simple analogy:

Image = Class
Container = Object

Or:

Image = Recipe
Container = Prepared dish

You create an image once and can create many containers from it.

7. Dockerfile

A Dockerfile is a text file containing instructions that Docker uses to build an image.

A simple Python Dockerfile might look like:

FROM python:3.12

WORKDIR /app

COPY requirements.txt .

RUN pip install -r requirements.txt

COPY . .

CMD ["python", "app.py"]

Let's understand it line by line.

FROM
FROM python:3.12

This specifies the base image.

Docker will start with a Python 3.12 environment.

WORKDIR
WORKDIR /app

This sets the working directory inside the image/container.

COPY
COPY requirements.txt .

This copies the dependency file into the image.

Then:

COPY . .

copies the application files.

RUN
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt

This executes a command while building the image.

CMD
CMD ["python", "app.py"]

This defines the default command executed when the container starts.

Docker documents FROM, RUN, COPY, WORKDIR, and CMD among the common Dockerfile instructions.

8. Building a Docker Image

Suppose your project looks like:

myapp/
│
├── app.py
├── requirements.txt
└── Dockerfile

You can build an image:

docker build -t myapp .

Here:

docker build

means build an image.

-t myapp

gives the image a name/tag.

.

means the current directory is the build context.

Docker uses the Dockerfile and files available in that build context to construct the image.

9. Running a Container

After building the image:

docker run myapp

Docker creates and starts a container from the image.

The flow is:

Dockerfile
    ↓
docker build
    ↓
Docker Image
    ↓
docker run
    ↓
Docker Container
    ↓
Application Running

This is the fundamental Docker workflow.

10. Useful Docker Commands

Some basic commands are:

Check Docker version
docker --version
List images
docker images
Run a container
docker run myapp
List running containers
docker ps
List all containers
docker ps -a
Stop a container
docker stop <container-id>
Start a stopped container
docker start <container-id>
Remove a container
docker rm <container-id>
Remove an image
docker rmi <image-id>

These commands allow developers to manage the basic lifecycle of Docker images and containers. Docker's documentation also uses docker ps for viewing running containers and docker stop for stopping them.

11. Docker Ports

Suppose your application runs on port 5000 inside the container.

The application is isolated inside the container, so you need to publish the port to access it from your machine.

For example:

docker run -p 5000:5000 myapp

The format is:

host-port : container-port

So:

5000:5000

means:

Your Computer
localhost:5000
       ↓
Docker Container
port 5000
       ↓
Application

Docker can publish container ports to the host so that applications can be accessed externally.

12. Docker Volumes

Containers are designed to be replaceable.

If important data exists only inside a container and that container is deleted, that data can disappear.

For persistent data, Docker provides volumes.

For example, a database container may use a volume:

Database Container
       ↓
Docker Volume
       ↓
Persistent Data

Even if you remove the container, the volume can preserve the data.

This is particularly important for:

databases
uploaded files
application data
logs
persistent storage

Docker supports storage mechanisms for persisting data outside the writable container layer.

13. Docker Networks

Containers often need to communicate with each other.

Imagine a web application consisting of:

Frontend
   ↓
Backend API
   ↓
Database

Each could run in its own container:

Frontend Container
        ↓
Backend Container
        ↓
Database Container

Docker networks allow these containers to communicate.

For example:

frontend
   │
   │ HTTP
   ↓
backend
   │
   │ database connection
   ↓
mysql

This separation is useful in microservice architectures.

14. Docker Compose

Real applications often need more than one container.

For example:

React Frontend
      +
Node.js Backend
      +
MySQL
      +
Redis

Running each container manually can become inconvenient.

Docker Compose allows you to define multi-container applications in a Compose file.

Conceptually:

docker-compose.yml
        ↓
 ┌──────┼─────────┐
 ↓      ↓         ↓
Web   Backend   Database

You can define:

services
networks
volumes
environment variables
ports

Then start the application stack using Docker Compose.

Docker's current learning path includes Compose specifically for multi-container applications.

15. Example Docker Compose Application

Imagine an application with:

Frontend
Backend
MySQL

A simplified Compose file might look like:

services:

  frontend:
    build: ./frontend
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"

  backend:
    build: ./backend
    ports:
      - "5000:5000"

  database:
    image: mysql:8

Now instead of manually starting three containers, you can manage the application as one multi-service stack.

The architecture becomes:

                  Docker Compose
                        │
          ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
          ↓             ↓             ↓
      Frontend       Backend       MySQL
      Container      Container     Container
16. Docker Registry

A Docker registry is a place where Docker images can be stored and distributed.

One popular registry is Docker Hub.

The workflow becomes:

Developer
   ↓
Dockerfile
   ↓
docker build
   ↓
Image
   ↓
docker push
   ↓
Docker Registry
   ↓
docker pull
   ↓
Production Server

This allows teams to share container images.

Docker documentation describes a registry as a place where Docker images are stored, and Docker Hub is the default public registry used by Docker in many workflows.

17. Docker Image Tags

Images can have tags.

For example:

myapp:1.0
myapp:2.0
myapp:latest

A tag helps identify a particular version.

For production systems, version-specific tags are often preferable to relying only on latest.

For example:

company/backend:1.4.2

is much clearer than:

company/backend:latest

because you know exactly which version you're deploying.

18. Docker and CI/CD

Docker is very useful in CI/CD pipelines.

Imagine a development workflow:

Developer
    ↓
Git Push
    ↓
GitHub
    ↓
CI Pipeline
    ↓
Build Docker Image
    ↓
Run Tests
    ↓
Push Image
    ↓
Deploy

Because the application is packaged consistently, the same image can move through:

Development
      ↓
Testing
      ↓
Staging
      ↓
Production

Docker specifically highlights containers as useful for continuous integration and continuous delivery workflows.

19. Docker in Machine Learning

Docker is also very useful for Machine Learning and AI projects.

Suppose an ML project requires:

Python 3.12
PyTorch
Transformers
CUDA
FastAPI
NumPy
Pandas

Installing all of these manually can cause environment problems.

Docker can package the environment:

Docker Image
│
├── Python
├── PyTorch
├── Transformers
├── NumPy
├── Pandas
├── FastAPI
└── ML Application

Then the same environment can be used during development and deployment.

For ML teams, this can be particularly useful when multiple developers need compatible environments.

20. Docker for Microservices

Docker fits naturally with microservice architectures.

Instead of building one huge application:

Large Monolithic Application

you can separate services:

                Application
                     │
        ┌────────────┼─────────────┐
        ↓            ↓             ↓
   User Service  Payment       Notification
                  Service        Service
        ↓            ↓             ↓
   Container      Container     Container

Each service can have:

its own dependencies
its own image
its own container
its own deployment lifecycle

This makes Docker useful for distributed systems.

21. Docker Security

Containers provide isolation, but Docker containers should not automatically be considered completely secure.

Developers should follow security practices such as:

use trusted base images
keep images updated
scan images for vulnerabilities
avoid unnecessary packages
don't store secrets directly in Dockerfiles
use non-root users where appropriate
limit container permissions
avoid exposing unnecessary ports
use minimal base images where practical

For example, instead of running an application as root, Docker's documentation demonstrates using a dedicated application user in Dockerfiles.

22. Dockerfile Best Practices

A good Dockerfile should be:

small
reproducible
secure
easy to understand
efficient to rebuild

For example, instead of copying everything immediately:

COPY . .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt

you can first copy dependency files:

COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt

COPY . .

Why?

Docker builds images in layers and can reuse cached layers when earlier instructions haven't changed.

If your source code changes but requirements.txt doesn't, Docker may be able to reuse the dependency-installation layer.

This can make builds faster.

23. Multi-Stage Builds

For some applications, you don't need development tools in the final production image.

For example:

Stage 1
Build Application
     ↓
Stage 2
Production Image

The first stage can contain:

compilers
development dependencies
build tools

The final stage contains only what is needed to run the application.

This can produce smaller and cleaner production images.

Docker's current documentation includes multi-stage builds as a technique for optimizing image construction.

24. Docker and Kubernetes

Docker and Kubernetes are related, but they are not the same thing.

Docker primarily provides tools for building and running containers.

Kubernetes is a platform for managing containerized workloads across clusters.

A simplified relationship is:

Docker
│
├── Build Image
├── Run Container
├── Manage Images
└── Container Development
             ↓
        Kubernetes
             ↓
   Manage many workloads
             ↓
    Multiple Machines

Kubernetes can manage things such as:

scaling
service discovery
deployments
health checks
container scheduling
rolling updates

So you can think:

Docker helps package and run applications; Kubernetes helps operate containerized applications at scale.

25. Docker's Complete Workflow

A typical Docker development lifecycle looks like this:

1. Write Application
        ↓
2. Create Dockerfile
        ↓
3. docker build
        ↓
4. Docker Image
        ↓
5. docker run
        ↓
6. Container
        ↓
7. Test Application
        ↓
8. docker tag
        ↓
9. docker push
        ↓
10. Container Registry
        ↓
11. Production

This workflow is one of the major reasons Docker became popular in modern application development.

26. A Simple Real-World Example

Imagine a company develops an employee learning platform.

The platform contains:

Next.js Frontend
Node.js Backend
MySQL Database
Redis

Without containers, developers might need to install all of these locally.

With Docker:

                 LMS Application
                       │
          ┌────────────┼────────────┐
          ↓            ↓            ↓
       Frontend      Backend       MySQL
       Container     Container     Container
                       │
                       ↓
                     Redis
                    Container

Docker Compose can define these services.

Now a developer can clone the project and start the environment using the project's container configuration instead of manually installing every dependency.

This creates a much more consistent development environment.

27. Common Docker Mistakes

Beginners often make several mistakes.

Mistake 1: Using huge images

A large image takes more storage and can take longer to transfer.

Mistake 2: Storing secrets in Dockerfiles

Never put things such as:

API_KEY=secret
PASSWORD=123456

directly into an image.

Mistake 3: Running everything as root

Use an appropriate non-root user when possible.

Mistake 4: Treating containers like virtual machines

Containers are not complete virtual machines.

Mistake 5: Storing database data only inside the container

Use persistent storage.

Mistake 6: Using latest everywhere

Versioned image tags make deployments easier to reproduce.

Mistake 7: Putting unnecessary files into the build context

A .dockerignore file can prevent unnecessary files from being sent to the builder.

28. Docker in Simple Words

If you remember only five things, remember these:

1. Dockerfile

Instructions for building an image.

2. Image

Package containing everything needed to run an application.

3. Container

Running instance of an image.

4. Registry

Place where images are stored and shared.

5. Docker Compose

Tool for managing applications made of multiple containers.

The basic relationship is:

                 Dockerfile
                     │
                     │ docker build
                     ↓
                Docker Image
                     │
                     │ docker run
                     ↓
               Docker Container
                     │
                     ↓
              Running Application
29. Final Takeaway

Docker is fundamentally about packaging applications consistently and running them in isolated environments.

Instead of saying:

"Install Python 3.12, install these 20 libraries, configure these environment variables, install this system dependency, and then run the application."

you can define the environment in a Dockerfile and build an image.

That image can then be used to create containers.

The overall idea is:

Application
    +
Dependencies
    +
Runtime
    +
Configuration
        ↓
    Docker Image
        ↓
    Container
        ↓
Running Application

This makes applications easier to develop, test, share, and deploy. Docker's official learning path covers the same progression: containers and images first, then Dockerfiles, building images, publishing them, and multi-container applications with Compose.

learningContents.description:
Docker: A Simple Guide to Containers and Application Deployment

Docker is one of the most widely used tools for modern software development. It helps developers package an application together with everything it needs to run and then execute that application in an isolated environment called a container.

The main problem Docker solves is simple:

“It works on my machine, but it doesn't work on yours.”

A developer may build an application using a particular version of Python, Node.js, Java, libraries, environment variables, and system dependencies. When another developer runs the same application on a different machine, something may fail because the environment is different.

Docker solves this by allowing the application and its dependencies to be packaged into a standardized image and run as a container. Docker describes a container as a runnable instance of an image, while an image is a standardized package containing the files, binaries, libraries, and configuration needed to run an application.

1. What Is Docker?

Docker is a platform for developing, shipping, and running applications.

Instead of installing everything directly on your computer, you can package your application into a Docker image.

For example, imagine you have a Python application.

Without Docker, your machine might need:

Python 3.12
Flask
NumPy
Pandas
specific operating-system libraries
environment variables
your application code

You would have to install all of these manually.

With Docker, you can describe the environment in a Dockerfile:

Python
   +
Libraries
   +
Application Code
   +
Configuration
       ↓
   Docker Image
       ↓
   Container
       ↓
Running Application

The result is a much more consistent environment between development, testing, and production.

Docker's platform is designed around packaging applications into containers, which can then be developed, tested, shared, and deployed across different environments.

2. Why Do We Need Docker?

Before understanding Docker technically, it is useful to understand the problem it solves.

Imagine a team building an AI application.

Developer A has:

Python 3.12
PyTorch 2.x
FastAPI
NumPy
CUDA libraries

Developer B has:

Python 3.10
Different PyTorch version
Different NumPy version
Different OS libraries

The application works on A's machine but fails on B's machine.

This can happen because of:

different programming-language versions
different library versions
missing dependencies
operating-system differences
configuration differences
environment-variable differences

Docker allows the team to define the environment once and package it.

Then:

Developer Machine
       ↓
Docker Container

Testing Server
       ↓
Docker Container

Cloud Server
       ↓
Docker Container

The application runs inside a controlled environment rather than depending heavily on what is installed on the host.

3. Docker vs Virtual Machines

Docker containers are often compared with virtual machines.

A traditional virtual-machine architecture looks like:

Physical Machine
       ↓
Host Operating System
       ↓
Hypervisor
       ↓
Virtual Machine
       ↓
Guest Operating System
       ↓
Application

A Docker architecture is generally more lightweight:

Physical Machine
       ↓
Host Operating System
       ↓
Docker Engine
       ↓
Container
       ↓
Application

A virtual machine normally includes an entire guest operating system.

A container shares the host's operating-system kernel while isolating processes, filesystems, networking, and other resources.

Docker uses Linux kernel technologies such as namespaces and cgroups to provide isolation and resource control.

This is one reason containers can be lightweight compared with full virtual machines.

4. What Is a Container?

A container is a running instance of a Docker image.

Think of an image as a blueprint and a container as the running thing created from that blueprint.

For example:

Docker Image
     ↓
     ↓ docker run
     ↓
Docker Container

Suppose you have an image called:

my-python-app

You can create a container from it:

docker run my-python-app

Docker starts a container based on the image.

You can have multiple containers created from the same image:

             Docker Image
                  │
       ┌──────────┼──────────┐
       ↓          ↓          ↓
 Container 1  Container 2  Container 3

Each container can have its own configuration, network settings, storage, and lifecycle.

5. What Is a Docker Image?

A Docker image is a read-only package used to create containers.

It contains everything required for an application to run, such as:

application code
runtime
libraries
dependencies
configuration
filesystem content

Docker images are built in layers. Each Dockerfile instruction can contribute a layer, and Docker can reuse unchanged layers when rebuilding an image.

For example:

Base Python Image
        ↓
Install Dependencies
        ↓
Copy Application
        ↓
Configure Application
        ↓
Docker Image

This layered structure also helps Docker use build cache efficiently.

6. Image vs Container

This is one of the most important concepts to understand.

Image	Container
Blueprint/template	Running instance
Read-only	Has a writable runtime layer
Used to create containers	Runs the application
Can be stored in a registry	Runs on a Docker host
Doesn't represent a running process	Represents a running process

A simple analogy:

Image = Class
Container = Object

Or:

Image = Recipe
Container = Prepared dish

You create an image once and can create many containers from it.

7. Dockerfile

A Dockerfile is a text file containing instructions that Docker uses to build an image.

A simple Python Dockerfile might look like:

FROM python:3.12

WORKDIR /app

COPY requirements.txt .

RUN pip install -r requirements.txt

COPY . .

CMD ["python", "app.py"]

Let's understand it line by line.

FROM
FROM python:3.12

This specifies the base image.

Docker will start with a Python 3.12 environment.

WORKDIR
WORKDIR /app

This sets the working directory inside the image/container.

COPY
COPY requirements.txt .

This copies the dependency file into the image.

Then:

COPY . .

copies the application files.

RUN
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt

This executes a command while building the image.

CMD
CMD ["python", "app.py"]

This defines the default command executed when the container starts.

Docker documents FROM, RUN, COPY, WORKDIR, and CMD among the common Dockerfile instructions.

8. Building a Docker Image

Suppose your project looks like:

myapp/
│
├── app.py
├── requirements.txt
└── Dockerfile

You can build an image:

docker build -t myapp .

Here:

docker build

means build an image.

-t myapp

gives the image a name/tag.

.

means the current directory is the build context.

Docker uses the Dockerfile and files available in that build context to construct the image.

9. Running a Container

After building the image:

docker run myapp

Docker creates and starts a container from the image.

The flow is:

Dockerfile
    ↓
docker build
    ↓
Docker Image
    ↓
docker run
    ↓
Docker Container
    ↓
Application Running

This is the fundamental Docker workflow.

10. Useful Docker Commands

Some basic commands are:

Check Docker version
docker --version
List images
docker images
Run a container
docker run myapp
List running containers
docker ps
List all containers
docker ps -a
Stop a container
docker stop <container-id>
Start a stopped container
docker start <container-id>
Remove a container
docker rm <container-id>
Remove an image
docker rmi <image-id>

These commands allow developers to manage the basic lifecycle of Docker images and containers. Docker's documentation also uses docker ps for viewing running containers and docker stop for stopping them.

11. Docker Ports

Suppose your application runs on port 5000 inside the container.

The application is isolated inside the container, so you need to publish the port to access it from your machine.

For example:

docker run -p 5000:5000 myapp

The format is:

host-port : container-port

So:

5000:5000

means:

Your Computer
localhost:5000
       ↓
Docker Container
port 5000
       ↓
Application

Docker can publish container ports to the host so that applications can be accessed externally.

12. Docker Volumes

Containers are designed to be replaceable.

If important data exists only inside a container and that container is deleted, that data can disappear.

For persistent data, Docker provides volumes.

For example, a database container may use a volume:

Database Container
       ↓
Docker Volume
       ↓
Persistent Data

Even if you remove the container, the volume can preserve the data.

This is particularly important for:

databases
uploaded files
application data
logs
persistent storage

Docker supports storage mechanisms for persisting data outside the writable container layer.

13. Docker Networks

Containers often need to communicate with each other.

Imagine a web application consisting of:

Frontend
   ↓
Backend API
   ↓
Database

Each could run in its own container:

Frontend Container
        ↓
Backend Container
        ↓
Database Container

Docker networks allow these containers to communicate.

For example:

frontend
   │
   │ HTTP
   ↓
backend
   │
   │ database connection
   ↓
mysql

This separation is useful in microservice architectures.

14. Docker Compose

Real applications often need more than one container.

For example:

React Frontend
      +
Node.js Backend
      +
MySQL
      +
Redis

Running each container manually can become inconvenient.

Docker Compose allows you to define multi-container applications in a Compose file.

Conceptually:

docker-compose.yml
        ↓
 ┌──────┼─────────┐
 ↓      ↓         ↓
Web   Backend   Database

You can define:

services
networks
volumes
environment variables
ports

Then start the application stack using Docker Compose.

Docker's current learning path includes Compose specifically for multi-container applications.

15. Example Docker Compose Application

Imagine an application with:

Frontend
Backend
MySQL

A simplified Compose file might look like:

services:

  frontend:
    build: ./frontend
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"

  backend:
    build: ./backend
    ports:
      - "5000:5000"

  database:
    image: mysql:8

Now instead of manually starting three containers, you can manage the application as one multi-service stack.

The architecture becomes:

                  Docker Compose
                        │
          ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
          ↓             ↓             ↓
      Frontend       Backend       MySQL
      Container      Container     Container
16. Docker Registry

A Docker registry is a place where Docker images can be stored and distributed.

One popular registry is Docker Hub.

The workflow becomes:

Developer
   ↓
Dockerfile
   ↓
docker build
   ↓
Image
   ↓
docker push
   ↓
Docker Registry
   ↓
docker pull
   ↓
Production Server

This allows teams to share container images.

Docker documentation describes a registry as a place where Docker images are stored, and Docker Hub is the default public registry used by Docker in many workflows.

17. Docker Image Tags

Images can have tags.

For example:

myapp:1.0
myapp:2.0
myapp:latest

A tag helps identify a particular version.

For production systems, version-specific tags are often preferable to relying only on latest.

For example:

company/backend:1.4.2

is much clearer than:

company/backend:latest

because you know exactly which version you're deploying.

18. Docker and CI/CD

Docker is very useful in CI/CD pipelines.

Imagine a development workflow:

Developer
    ↓
Git Push
    ↓
GitHub
    ↓
CI Pipeline
    ↓
Build Docker Image
    ↓
Run Tests
    ↓
Push Image
    ↓
Deploy

Because the application is packaged consistently, the same image can move through:

Development
      ↓
Testing
      ↓
Staging
      ↓
Production

Docker specifically highlights containers as useful for continuous integration and continuous delivery workflows.

19. Docker in Machine Learning

Docker is also very useful for Machine Learning and AI projects.

Suppose an ML project requires:

Python 3.12
PyTorch
Transformers
CUDA
FastAPI
NumPy
Pandas

Installing all of these manually can cause environment problems.

Docker can package the environment:

Docker Image
│
├── Python
├── PyTorch
├── Transformers
├── NumPy
├── Pandas
├── FastAPI
└── ML Application

Then the same environment can be used during development and deployment.

For ML teams, this can be particularly useful when multiple developers need compatible environments.

20. Docker for Microservices

Docker fits naturally with microservice architectures.

Instead of building one huge application:

Large Monolithic Application

you can separate services:

                Application
                     │
        ┌────────────┼─────────────┐
        ↓            ↓             ↓
   User Service  Payment       Notification
                  Service        Service
        ↓            ↓             ↓
   Container      Container     Container

Each service can have:

its own dependencies
its own image
its own container
its own deployment lifecycle

This makes Docker useful for distributed systems.

21. Docker Security

Containers provide isolation, but Docker containers should not automatically be considered completely secure.

Developers should follow security practices such as:

use trusted base images
keep images updated
scan images for vulnerabilities
avoid unnecessary packages
don't store secrets directly in Dockerfiles
use non-root users where appropriate
limit container permissions
avoid exposing unnecessary ports
use minimal base images where practical

For example, instead of running an application as root, Docker's documentation demonstrates using a dedicated application user in Dockerfiles.

22. Dockerfile Best Practices

A good Dockerfile should be:

small
reproducible
secure
easy to understand
efficient to rebuild

For example, instead of copying everything immediately:

COPY . .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt

you can first copy dependency files:

COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt

COPY . .

Why?

Docker builds images in layers and can reuse cached layers when earlier instructions haven't changed.

If your source code changes but requirements.txt doesn't, Docker may be able to reuse the dependency-installation layer.

This can make builds faster.

23. Multi-Stage Builds

For some applications, you don't need development tools in the final production image.

For example:

Stage 1
Build Application
     ↓
Stage 2
Production Image

The first stage can contain:

compilers
development dependencies
build tools

The final stage contains only what is needed to run the application.

This can produce smaller and cleaner production images.

Docker's current documentation includes multi-stage builds as a technique for optimizing image construction.

24. Docker and Kubernetes

Docker and Kubernetes are related, but they are not the same thing.

Docker primarily provides tools for building and running containers.

Kubernetes is a platform for managing containerized workloads across clusters.

A simplified relationship is:

Docker
│
├── Build Image
├── Run Container
├── Manage Images
└── Container Development
             ↓
        Kubernetes
             ↓
   Manage many workloads
             ↓
    Multiple Machines

Kubernetes can manage things such as:

scaling
service discovery
deployments
health checks
container scheduling
rolling updates

So you can think:

Docker helps package and run applications; Kubernetes helps operate containerized applications at scale.

25. Docker's Complete Workflow

A typical Docker development lifecycle looks like this:

1. Write Application
        ↓
2. Create Dockerfile
        ↓
3. docker build
        ↓
4. Docker Image
        ↓
5. docker run
        ↓
6. Container
        ↓
7. Test Application
        ↓
8. docker tag
        ↓
9. docker push
        ↓
10. Container Registry
        ↓
11. Production

This workflow is one of the major reasons Docker became popular in modern application development.

26. A Simple Real-World Example

Imagine a company develops an employee learning platform.

The platform contains:

Next.js Frontend
Node.js Backend
MySQL Database
Redis

Without containers, developers might need to install all of these locally.

With Docker:

                 LMS Application
                       │
          ┌────────────┼────────────┐
          ↓            ↓            ↓
       Frontend      Backend       MySQL
       Container     Container     Container
                       │
                       ↓
                     Redis
                    Container

Docker Compose can define these services.

Now a developer can clone the project and start the environment using the project's container configuration instead of manually installing every dependency.

This creates a much more consistent development environment.

27. Common Docker Mistakes

Beginners often make several mistakes.

Mistake 1: Using huge images

A large image takes more storage and can take longer to transfer.

Mistake 2: Storing secrets in Dockerfiles

Never put things such as:

API_KEY=secret
PASSWORD=123456

directly into an image.

Mistake 3: Running everything as root

Use an appropriate non-root user when possible.

Mistake 4: Treating containers like virtual machines

Containers are not complete virtual machines.

Mistake 5: Storing database data only inside the container

Use persistent storage.

Mistake 6: Using latest everywhere

Versioned image tags make deployments easier to reproduce.

Mistake 7: Putting unnecessary files into the build context

A .dockerignore file can prevent unnecessary files from being sent to the builder.

28. Docker in Simple Words

If you remember only five things, remember these:

1. Dockerfile

Instructions for building an image.

2. Image

Package containing everything needed to run an application.

3. Container

Running instance of an image.

4. Registry

Place where images are stored and shared.

5. Docker Compose

Tool for managing applications made of multiple containers.

The basic relationship is:

                 Dockerfile
                     │
                     │ docker build
                     ↓
                Docker Image
                     │
                     │ docker run
                     ↓
               Docker Container
                     │
                     ↓
              Running Application
29. Final Takeaway

Docker is fundamentally about packaging applications consistently and running them in isolated environments.

Instead of saying:

"Install Python 3.12, install these 20 libraries, configure these environment variables, install this system dependency, and then run the application."

you can define the environment in a Dockerfile and build an image.

That image can then be used to create containers.

The overall idea is:

Application
    +
Dependencies
    +
Runtime
    +
Configuration
        ↓
    Docker Image
        ↓
    Container
        ↓
Running Application

This makes applications easier to develop, test, share, and deploy. Docker's official learning path covers the same progression: containers and images first, then Dockerfiles, building images, publishing them, and multi-container applications with Compose.
